extracted.intended_audience: graduate students, postdocs, early-career mathematicians and undergraduates considering research careers
extracted.subtask_description: Collection of practical career and research-advice guidelines for students and early-career researchers in mathematics, organised by career stage (primary school through postdoc) and covering skills, habits, and choices that affect academic success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work hard
rubrics_metrics.description: It is important to work hard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as a primary graduate-level expectation; presented as a blunt essential alongside other professional habits (see also 'work professionally'). No specific quantitative metric given, but framed as a baseline for research progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work professionally
rubrics_metrics.description: Work professionally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paired with 'work hard' as a core expectation for graduate students; implies reliable, organized, responsible research conduct (e.g., meeting commitments, managing time, communicating results).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enjoy your work
rubrics_metrics.description: But it is also important to enjoy your work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advises balancing effort/professionalism with personal satisfaction to sustain long-term research productivity and creativity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think ahead to understand the way forward
rubrics_metrics.description: Think ahead to understand the way forward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan research direction strategically; anticipate steps needed to reach longer-term goals rather than only reacting to immediate tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask yourself dumb questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask yourself dumb questions to understand the way before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use naïve or basic questioning as a tool to clarify understanding of a problem and its context; helps build intuition before technical work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend talks and conferences (even unrelated ones)
rubrics_metrics.description: Attend talks and conferences, even those not directly related to your own work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expose yourself to broader ideas and techniques; networking and serendipitous insights can arise from peripheral areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Talk to your advisor but take initiative
rubrics_metrics.description: Talk to your advisor, but also take the initiative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine regular communication with proactive problem selection and independent work; don't rely solely on advisor direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't prematurely obsess on a single 'big problem' or 'big theory'
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t prematurely obsess on a single 'big problem' or 'big theory'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid locking into one grand goal too early; diversify projects until you have sufficient tools and perspective to pursue large undertakings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write down what you've done and make your work available
rubrics_metrics.description: Write down what you’ve done, and make your work available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep records of progress, draft papers, circulate preprints; active dissemination is part of building a research profile (see linked advice on how to write and submit papers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn and relearn your field; don't fear learning outside it
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn and relearn your field, but don’t be afraid to learn things outside your field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain up-to-date knowledge in core areas and also cross-train in adjacent fields to gain new tools and perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn limitations of your tools and the power of others' tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn the limitations of your tools, but also learn the power of other mathematician’s tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be honest about what techniques can and cannot do; study alternative methods to expand your problem-solving repertoire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continually aim just beyond your current range
rubrics_metrics.description: You should continually aim just beyond your current range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Push yourself incrementally into slightly harder problems/techniques to grow capability without overreaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be flexible and patient in research
rubrics_metrics.description: In your research, be both flexible and patient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt to setbacks and changing directions; allow time for ideas to mature and for progress to accumulate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Travel and present research when given the opportunity
rubrics_metrics.description: You should definitely travel and present your research if given the opportunity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use visits and talks to get feedback, meet potential collaborators, and increase visibility; balance travel with other responsibilities and be selective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider your audience; talks are not the same as papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Be considerate of your audience; talks are not the same as papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor exposition and level of detail to the venue and audience; oral presentations require clarity and different emphasis than written work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be sceptical of your own work; use the wastebasket
rubrics_metrics.description: Be sceptical of your own work, and don’t be afraid to use the wastebasket.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critically evaluate partial ideas; discard approaches that are unpromising rather than spending excessive time polishing them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Batch low-intensity tasks together
rubrics_metrics.description: Batch low-intensity tasks together to take advantage of economies of scale and to reduce distraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Group email/admin/other small chores into blocks so they interrupt deep work less often; a time-management tactic recommended for researchers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t base career decisions on glamour or fame; study at different places
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t base career decisions on glamour or fame. But you should study at different places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid choosing institutions solely for prestige; still seek varied experiences and environments to broaden training and opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build your own network of colleagues and collaborators
rubrics_metrics.description: Build your own network of colleagues and collaborators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate relationships beyond your immediate advisor/group to find collaborators, mentors, and job opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Programming skills: useful but field-dependent
rubrics_metrics.description: Programming is a useful general skill to have, but in most areas of pure mathematics it is not necessary beyond rudimentary levels; more essential in numerical/applied areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acquire programming skills proportional to the needs of your subfield; basic familiarity with computational tools (Maple, Mathematica, etc.) is typically beneficial.

rubrics_metrics.name: There is more to mathematics than grades/exams/methods and than rigour/proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Note that there is more to maths than grades and exams and methods; there is also more to maths than rigour and proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasises broader development (problem solving, intuition, exposition, creativity) rather than solely formal correctness or grades.

rubrics_metrics.name: You do not have to be a genius to succeed
rubrics_metrics.description: Does one have to be a genius to succeed at maths? (Implicit answer: no.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages students that effort, training, and good habits often matter more than innate brilliance; do not let myth of genius deter persistence.
